top.title: Lead Lattice: an AI scientist that trains a separate model for every one of the 4,095 ECG lead subsets on one GPU
top.description: A general hypothesis engine. An LLM planner writes experiments as structured specs (lead mask, label, architecture, seeds). A compiler merges compatible specs into one vectorised population of tiny 1-D CNNs and trains them together on one GPU. The planner reads the results and proposes the next round. The demonstration question: which subsets of the 12 standard leads keep diagnostic performance for each PTB-XL superclass (MI, conduction disturbance, hypertrophy, ST/T change, normal), and what is the smallest set for each? The hardware result is a measured profile of a typical AI-scientist workload, thousands of small concurrent jobs: models trained per GPU-hour run four ways (sequential loop, many processes, MPS, one vmap population), the population size where throughput saturates, SM use and memory per model. The judge adds one further claim, and it is the main defence against prior art: compare the cheap one-model shortcut (a single masked model scoring every subset, as Li and Tao 2026 do) against the ground truth of a model trained per subset, which only packing makes affordable.
top.scores: compute-hardware 4, AI-scientist loop 4, biotech 4, visual 4, sponsor 4, feasibility 5, honesty 5 (total 30/35)
top.verified: Verified: PTB-XL benchmark superdiagnostic macro AUC resnet1d_wang 0.930, xresnet1d101 0.928, lstm 0.927, fcn_wang 0.925, inception1d 0.921 (https://github.com/helme/ecg_ptbxl_benchmarking). CinC 2021 lead sets were 12, 6, 4 (I, II, III, V2), 3 (I, II, V2) and 2 (I, II), and teams' scores changed by less than 2% from 12 to 2 leads. That figure is the Challenge metric, not AUC (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9469795). Front. Cardiovasc. Med. 2024 reports 12-lead 93.2%, lead I 85.1%, I+II 90.6% and 8 leads 92.95%. CORRECTION: those are averages over 20 diagnostic classes, not the 5 superclasses (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10901971). Closest prior art: Li and Tao 2026 (arXiv 2608.26827, v2 7 Sep 2026) score every subset of size k in {1,2,3,4,6,8}, 2,212 candidates per evaluator. They score with one masked ResNet1D or a logistic model rather than training per subset, select by NLL, Brier or ECE, and publish no per-subset AUC map over all 4,095 (https://arxiv.org/html/2608.26827). Robroek et al.: collocating training jobs gives up to 4x throughput, and MPS is best for a single user (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06018). HiveMind (Microsoft): up to 10x on P100/V100 for multi-model work. Simply launching models' ops in parallel gives little gain, because of memory-bound kernels and launch overhead (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/accelerating-deep-learning-workloads-through-efficient-multi-model-execution/). PyTorch ensembling uses stack_module_state, functional_call and vmap, with in_dims=(0,0,None) for a shared minibatch (https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/ensembling.html). BatchNorm fails under vmap: use GroupNorm or track_running_stats=False (https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.5/func.batch_norm.html). UNVERIFIED: the ModelBatch 9.2x figure, and compute cost. The judge's own estimate, not measured: about 1e14 FLOPs per tiny model for 20 epochs, so the full lattice is hours, not minutes, on one GPU, and seeds must be budgeted.
top.main_risk: A judge says it is just batching, and that a single masked model scores all subsets in seconds, so the GPU is optional. Answer it with the measured masked-model-against-ground-truth rank agreement: if the shortcut misranks the minimal subsets, the packed ground truth is needed; if it agrees, that is itself a useful cost result. The secondary risk is that a full 4,095 x multi-seed lattice does not fit overnight on one GPU. Mitigate with one seed over the full lattice and extra seeds only on the subsets the planner targets.
top.headline_metric: (1) Models trained per GPU-hour, vmap population against a sequential loop and against MPS on the same GPU, with the saturation population size. Full 4,095-subset lattice in X min against a projected Y h sequentially. (2) Spearman rank agreement between the one-model masked shortcut and per-subset trained ground truth, per superclass. (3) Reproduction: our 12-lead superdiagnostic macro AUC against 0.930 (resnet1d_wang), and the minimal lead set per superclass within 0.01 AUC of 12-lead, with seed CIs.

top.title: Starving Tensor Cores: pathology-slide AI scientist bounded by JPEG decode, not FLOPs (CAMELYON16)
top.description: An agent tests slide-level hypotheses for finding breast-cancer metastases in lymph-node whole-slide images: magnification, patch selection, top-k against attention pooling, encoder choice. It does so cheaply on cached patch embeddings, and a systems agent schedules the costly embedding extraction. The hardware result is a stage-by-stage throughput breakdown (decode, transfer, encoder, head). It tests whether moving JPEG decode from the CPU to the GPU's fixed-function hardware JPEG engine flips the pipeline from decode-bound to compute-bound, and at which encoder size. This is the most chip-native story of the four, and it has the best visual: a gigapixel slide with a live attention heatmap over the pathologist's outline.
top.scores: compute-hardware 5 (if the preconditions hold), AI-scientist loop 3, biotech 5, visual 5, sponsor 4, feasibility 2, honesty 4 (total 28/35)
top.verified: Verified: CAMELYON is on AWS Open Data in bucket camelyon-dataset (us-west-2), CC0, readable with --no-sign-request and no account (https://registry.opendata.aws/camelyon/). nvJPEG hardware backend is listed for Ampere (A100, A30), Hopper, Ada, Blackwell and Jetson Thor. It covers baseline single-scan JPEG only, and 4:1:0 and 4:1:1 chroma subsampling are unsupported (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/nvjpeg/index.html). The cuCIM README says cuslide is deprecated in favour of cuslide2 (ENABLE_CUSLIDE2=1), which does GPU TIFF decode through nvImageCodec 0.10 with nvJPEG, nvTIFF and nvJPEG2000. The README gives no speedup numbers and does not call it experimental (https://github.com/rapidsai/cucim). CORRECTION: the ideator's claim that cuslide2 is experimental is not supported by the README. UNVERIFIED: that CAMELYON16 TIFF tiles are baseline JPEG at quality 80 to 90. The cited arXiv 2412.13137 abstract does not mention Camelyon16. Also unverified: which consumer Ada cards (RTX 4090, L4, L40S) actually expose the hardware decoder. TransMIL's ABMIL 0.876 and TransMIL 0.931 baselines were not re-opened here.
top.main_risk: Three preconditions can each break the story, and none is checked yet: the slides' compression must be baseline JPEG, the event GPU must have the hardware JPEG engine, and enough slides (the full set is about 900 GB per the ideator, unverified) must download from us-west-2 to London inside the weekend. 'WSI pipelines are I/O-bound' is also partly folklore and partly published (TRIDENT).
top.headline_metric: Tiles per second from slide to embedding: CPU decode with N workers against the GPU hardware-decode pipeline on the same GPU, plus the share of wall time spent in decode at two encoder sizes. Secondary: the agent's best MIL variant's test AUC against ABMIL near 0.876 on ResNet50-ImageNet features.

top.title: Which chip should score this mutation? Routing protein variant-effect inference across ESM-2 sizes and devices (ProteinGym)
top.description: An agent scores ProteinGym deep-mutational-scanning assays with ESM-2 at 8M to 3B parameters (15B optional) and with several scoring rules (wild-type marginal, masked marginal, pseudo-perplexity). On each available device it measures latency, throughput, memory and utilisation, and finds where the workload is memory-bound (big model, small batch) or compute-bound. It then learns a per-assay routing policy that sends each protein to the cheapest model and chip that loses no accuracy. Every run can be checked assay by assay against ProteinGym's published reference scores.
top.scores: compute-hardware 4 (3 if only one GPU type), AI-scientist loop 3, biotech 4, visual 4, sponsor 5, feasibility 4, honesty 3 (total 27/35)
top.verified: Verified from the ProteinGym summary CSV (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OATML-Markslab/ProteinGym/main/benchmarks/DMS_zero_shot/substitutions/Spearman/Summary_performance_DMS_substitutions_Spearman.csv): average Spearman for ESM2 8M 0.226, 35M 0.321, 150M 0.387, 650M 0.414, 3B 0.406, 15B 0.400; ESM-1v ensemble 0.407; top models AIDO Protein-RAG 16B 0.518, VenusREM 0.518, ProSST K=2048 0.507. Kantroo et al. 2024 estimate pseudo-perplexity in one forward pass, nearly as well as true pseudo-perplexity, with no runtime figure in the abstract (https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07265v1). UNVERIFIED: the ESM-2 15B memory need, which chip types the event provides, and the 'Scaling Down for Efficiency' paper.
top.main_risk: It overlaps the already-rejected angle of an AI scientist budgeting compute across cheap and expensive tiers. 'Medium ESM-2 is as good as large' is already visible in the published table. The distinct claim, a multi-device crossover, depends on the event providing two or more chip types.
top.headline_metric: GPU-seconds and device mix needed to reach within 0.01 average Spearman of the best ESM-2 configuration, against always running the largest model with masked marginal on the largest GPU. Sanity check: reproduction error of per-size Spearmans against 0.226 to 0.414.

top.title: Six Million Forward Passes: cheap genome-wide in-silico knockouts with Geneformer, checked against real Perturb-seq
top.description: An agent runs in-silico gene deletions with the open Geneformer model on K562 cells and compares each predicted embedding shift with the real CRISPRi knockdown from the Replogle genome-scale Perturb-seq screen. It looks for the gene classes where the foundation model beats a PCA or linear baseline. The hardware result is an inference-throughput study of millions of near-duplicate encoder passes: batch size, length-sorted batching, the attention kernel, and sharding across GPUs.
top.scores: compute-hardware 3, AI-scientist loop 3, biotech 5, visual 4, sponsor 3, feasibility 2, honesty 4 (total 24/35)
top.verified: Verified (https://huggingface.co/ctheodoris/Geneformer/discussions/508): a user reports about 60 h on one A100 40GB for max_ncells=1500 (forward_batch_size 256, nproc 16). The maintainer explains that all-gene deletion over up to 4,096 genes is about 6.1M forward passes. They advise bigger batches and parallel jobs per cell set via cell_inds_to_perturb, saying 'There will be no difference in the results as this is all performed as inference.' UNVERIFIED: the pertpy replogle_2022_k562_gwps loader page returned 404 at its new address. Also unverified: whether SDPA or flash attention works with the Geneformer perturber, and the Ahlmann-Eltze and Bendidi results, which were not re-opened here.
top.main_risk: Tokenising K562 and matching gene IDs takes hours. Comparing an embedding shift with an expression shift needs a mapping design that can sink the result. The likely science outcome, that the linear baseline wins, is already published. A judge may also say the CPU baseline makes the GPU optional.
top.headline_metric: In-silico perturbations per GPU-second after optimisation against the default perturber, set against the 60 h / 1,500-cell anecdote. Agreement with real knockdown direction for Geneformer against PCA, per gene class.

verdict.recommended: Lead Lattice (rank 1). The ideators supplied only four distinct candidates. None were duplicates, so there was nothing to merge, and the judge did not invent an unvetted fifth idea to fill the top 5. Lead Lattice wins because each of the four constraints rests on something checked rather than hoped for. Data: PTB-XL is open, about 1.7 GB per the ideator, and fits in GPU memory. Baselines: published 12-lead superdiagnostic AUCs (0.930 resnet1d_wang) and the CinC 2021 lead sets. Hardware result: a measured throughput curve for a packed population against sequential and MPS, which needs no special chip and so works on whatever GPU the event provides. Visual: a 4,095-node lattice that lights up live. The key change from the ideator's version is the defence against the closest prior art, Li and Tao 2026. They score up to 2,212 subsets with one masked model, select by NLL, Brier or ECE, and publish no per-subset trained AUC map. So lead the pitch with how well the cheap one-model shortcut ranks lead subsets against per-subset trained ground truth, which only GPU packing makes affordable. Do not claim the discovery that 2 leads suffice: CinC 2021 already showed a change of under 2% in the Challenge metric. Keep CAMELYON as the fallback, and adopt it instead only if within the first hour the team confirms that the event GPU has the hardware JPEG engine (A100, A30, Hopper, Ada or Blackwell per the nvJPEG docs) and that CAMELYON16 tiles are baseline JPEG. Avoid the excluded angles: no precision study, no roofline kernel tuning, no compute-budget tiers. Corrections to carry into the pitch: the Frontiers 2024 figures (93.2%, 85.1%, 90.6%) are averages over 20 diagnostic classes, not superclasses. The CinC 'less than 2%' is the Challenge score, not AUC. Expect a small 1-D CNN to land somewhat below 0.930 and report that gap honestly.
verdict.plan_28h:
Sat 11:00-13:00 (both engineers). Set up the environment. Download PTB-XL at 100 Hz, load all records once into a GPU tensor, and use the benchmark folds (train 1-8, val 9, test 10). Build a tiny 1-D CNN with GroupNorm, not BatchNorm, because BatchNorm breaks vmap. Time one sequential model. Medical student: list clinical hypotheses (inferior MI and II/III/aVF, anterior MI and V1-V4, limb-lead redundancy from Einthoven) and sketch the pitch.
Sat 13:00-17:00, engineer A. Build the population trainer: stack_module_state + functional_call + vmap, with one shared minibatch and a per-model lead mask. Correctness gate: packed model k must match the sequential model k (same seed) on its loss curve within tolerance. Sweep population size from 1 to 4,096 for models per GPU-hour, nvidia-smi dmon SM use, and memory per model. Add the MPS multi-process baseline.
Sat 13:00-17:00, engineer B. Build the engine: a JSON experiment-spec schema, an LLM planner on the provided credits, a compiler that merges specs into populations, and a results store with the per-superclass AUC and a CI. Also train the one-model masked shortcut (random lead dropout) that scores every subset.
Sat 17:00-23:00. Reproduce 12-lead superdiagnostic AUC against 0.930 and record the gap. Launch the full 4,095-subset lattice for seed 0 with checkpointing, so a kill resumes. Build the dashboard: a D3 Hasse lattice coloured by AUC with the planner's current hypothesis highlighted, plus sequential-against-packed GPU gauges and a models-per-minute counter, fed from the results file over a websocket.
Overnight. Lattice seed 0. Agent rounds 1-2: the planner proposes minimal-set and interaction hypotheses, and runs seeds 1-4 only on the targeted subsets.
Sun 08:00-12:00. Analysis: the minimal lead set per superclass within 0.01 AUC of 12-lead, with seed CIs. Spearman rank agreement of the masked shortcut against the trained ground truth, per superclass. The final throughput curve and saturation point. Agent round 3 recorded end to end for the demo. Stretch, only if ahead: one more plug-in, such as another PhysioNet task, to show the engine is domain-free.
Sun 12:00-15:00. Freeze the code. Script a live run of the 298 subsets with at most 3 leads (12+66+220) so the lattice fills on stage. The sequential gauge crawls beside it.
Sun 15:00-18:00. Medical student leads the pitch: clinical lead map, then the three numbers. Rehearse twice and keep a recorded fallback video.
Headline numbers to report, all measured at the event and none promised: (1) models per GPU-hour, packed against sequential and against MPS, with the saturation size, and the lattice in X min against Y h projected sequentially. (2) Masked-shortcut against ground-truth rank Spearman. (3) 12-lead AUC against 0.930, and the minimal lead set per superclass.
killed: No idea was killed outright: all four candidates survive as ranks 1-4, because the ideators sent only four. The entries below are framings dropped from those ideas.

Lead Lattice framed as discovering that two leads are nearly enough: CinC 2021 already reported under 2% Challenge-score change from 12 to 2 leads, and Li and Tao 2026 already evaluate up to 2,212 subsets with a masked model.
Citing the ModelBatch 9.2x speedup: not verified. The verifiable figure is HiveMind's 'up to 10x on P100 and V100', which also notes that naive parallel launches give little gain.

CAMELYON with the full roughly 900 GB download (size unverified) as the main path: the transfer from us-west-2 and the unverified JPEG compression of the slides make it too risky without an hour-1 go/no-go check.

Geneformer genome-wide screen as the science claim: linear and PCA baselines already match or beat foundation models in the papers the ideator cites, and the tokenisation plus the embedding-to-expression mapping is too risky for 28 hours.

ProteinGym 'medium ESM-2 beats large' as the headline: the public table already shows 650M (0.414) above 3B (0.406) and 15B (0.400), and cost-tier routing overlaps the rejected compute-budgeting angle.
ProteinGym on a single GPU type: without a second chip it reduces to a single-chip cost map, which loses its Callosum and Fractile relevance.
